blocks.content: Look at your car's dashboard for a second. It doesn't hand you a logbook of every spark plug firing or every drop of fuel burned. It shows you three or four live numbers: speed, fuel level, engine temperature. You glance down, you know instantly if something's off, and you move on.

That's exactly the job a metric does for your systems. Not a play by play of every single event like a log gives you, just a number, tracked over time, cheap enough to check every few seconds and act on immediately.
1. Introduction
A metric is a numeric measurement recorded over time. Requests served, bytes sent, milliseconds taken, connections open. Just numbers, sampled or incremented repeatedly, so you can watch them move.
1.1 What a metric actually is

Every metric has the same shape underneath: a name, a value, and a timestamp. "http_requests_total = 48213 at 10:02:15" is a metric. That's it. No message, no stack trace, no user id sitting in a giant text blob.

["Numeric, always a number you can add, average, or compare, never free text","Recorded over time, so you can draw a line through thousands of points and see a trend","Cheap to store, a counter bump costs almost nothing compared to writing a full log line","Built for aggregation, sum it across servers, average it across a minute, alert when it crosses a threshold"]
items: Numeric, always a number you can add, average, or compare, never free text
Recorded over time, so you can draw a line through thousands of points and see a trend
Cheap to store, a counter bump costs almost nothing compared to writing a full log line
Built for aggregation, sum it across servers, average it across a minute, alert when it crosses a threshold

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Metrics are what make dashboards and alerts possible in the first place. You can't put a million log lines on a graph and read it at a glance. You can put a million counter increments into one clean line.
1.2 Metrics versus logs

Logs and metrics both tell you what happened, but they answer different questions. A log tells you the story of one specific request: which user, which error, which stack trace. A metric tells you the shape of everything happening across the whole system.

{"headers":["Metrics","Logs"],"rows":[["Numbers over time","Text records per event"],["Cheap at high volume","Expensive to store and search at scale"],["Great for trends and alerting thresholds","Great for debugging one specific incident"],["Aggregated, no per request detail","Full per request detail"]]}
If you want to know whether your system is healthy right now, reach for metrics. If you want to know exactly why one request failed at 3:14am, reach for logs.
2. The four core metric types

Almost every metrics system, Prometheus included, gives you four building blocks. Pick the wrong one for the job and your dashboard either lies to you or just doesn't answer the question you actually have.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350358-533323441.png
blocks.alt: Four metric types side by side: counter, gauge, histogram, summary

blocks.content: 2.1 Counter
A counter is a value that only ever goes up. Total requests served, total errors thrown, total bytes sent. It resets to zero only when the process restarts, never in between.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350359-652062004.png
blocks.alt: A counter climbing upward over four points in time, never decreasing

blocks.content: A request counter incremented once on every single request handled is the textbook example. You never subtract from a counter. If you find yourself wanting to decrease one, you actually want a gauge.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Counters reset to zero when a process restarts or a pod gets rescheduled. Prometheus's rate() and increase() functions are built to handle that reset automatically, so don't try to detect resets by hand.
2.2 Gauge
A gauge is a value that can go up or down. Current memory usage, number of active connections, queue depth right now. Whatever the value is at the moment you look, that's what the gauge reports.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350359-494506874.png
blocks.alt: A gauge value rising and falling across four points in the day

blocks.content: Active database connections is a good gauge. It climbs when new connections open, drops when they close, and there's no meaningful running total to keep.
2.3 Histogram

A histogram observes a value, usually a duration, and sorts it into predefined buckets by range. Every request's response time gets counted into the bucket it falls in: under 50ms, under 200ms, under 1000ms, and so on.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350359-429630245.png
blocks.alt: Request latencies bucketed by range, most requests fast, a shrinking tail slower

blocks.content: Because the raw bucket counts are stored on the server, you can compute any percentile you want later, across any time window, even across multiple instances added together. That flexibility is the whole point of a histogram.
2.4 Summary

A summary looks similar on the surface, it's also about distributions of observed values, but the percentile math happens client side, inside your application process, before the number ever leaves it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396350360-784474356.png
blocks.alt: Histogram computes percentiles on the server, summary computes them on the client

blocks.content: {"headers":["Histogram","Summary"],"rows":[["Percentiles computed by the query engine (Prometheus)","Percentiles computed inside the app itself"],["Can be aggregated across instances after the fact","Cannot be meaningfully averaged across instances"],["Slightly more storage (raw buckets)","Slightly less storage (just the computed quantiles)"],["The default choice for most teams","Used when you need an exact quantile the app itself computes"]]}

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: You cannot average summary percentiles across five server instances and get a correct answer. p99 of averages is not the same number as the true p99. Histograms don't have this problem, which is why most teams default to histograms.
3. Why percentiles matter more than averages
blocks.text: 3. Why percentiles matter more than averages

blocks.content: This is the single most common mistake in production monitoring: staring at an average latency graph, seeing a flat healthy line, and having no idea that a meaningful slice of real users is having a miserable time.
3.1 How an average lies to you
blocks.text: 3.1 How an average lies to you

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351170-806994846.png
blocks.alt: An average latency that looks fine while p99 latency is badly hurting some users

blocks.title: The math behind the lie
blocks.text: Say your endpoint handles 100 requests. 99 of them return in 50ms. One of them, for whatever reason, takes 5000ms. The average across all 100 requests comes out to about 99ms, which looks perfectly fine on a dashboard. But that one request is real. If your traffic is a million requests a day, that same one percent tail is ten thousand people having a genuinely bad experience, every single day, invisible in the average.

blocks.content: Averages smear the outliers into the middle. The bigger your traffic, the more real people that tail represents, and the more it deserves your attention, not your dismissal.
3.2 p50, p95, p99 and what they actually tell you
blocks.text: 3.2 p50, p95, p99 and what they actually tell you

blocks.content: ["p50 (median), half your requests are faster than this, half are slower. Your typical experience.","p95, 95 out of 100 requests are faster than this. The slower end of normal.","p99, only 1 out of 100 requests is slower than this. Your worst common case, the one that tells you if something is quietly rotting."]
items: p50 (median), half your requests are faster than this, half are slower. Your typical experience.
p95, 95 out of 100 requests are faster than this. The slower end of normal.
p99, only 1 out of 100 requests is slower than this. Your worst common case, the one that tells you if something is quietly rotting.

blocks.content: Most teams set alerting thresholds on p95 or p99, not on the average, precisely because the average hides exactly the problem you're trying to catch.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: p99 on a low traffic endpoint is noisy. With only 100 requests an hour, one slow request due to a random blip can swing your p99 wildly. You need enough sample volume before a percentile means anything stable.
4. Instrumentation

Instrumentation is the practice of adding metric emission directly into your application code. It's not something a separate agent does for you by magic, someone on your team has to decide what's worth measuring and write the two or three lines that measure it.
4.1 What you actually add to the code
blocks.text: 4.1 What you actually add to the code

blocks.content: In practice this comes down to a small set of repeated patterns: a counter incremented once at the top or bottom of a request handler, and a histogram that observes how long the handler took, wrapped around the actual work.

["A request counter, incremented on every single request, tagged with route and status code","A duration histogram, observing how long each request took, from the moment it arrived to the moment the response was sent","A gauge for anything that fluctuates right now, like the number of jobs sitting in a queue"]
items: A request counter, incremented on every single request, tagged with route and status code
A duration histogram, observing how long each request took, from the moment it arrived to the moment the response was sent
A gauge for anything that fluctuates right now, like the number of jobs sitting in a queue

blocks.content: 4.2 Where instrumentation belongs

The cleanest place to add this is a single piece of middleware that wraps every request, not scattered calls sprinkled through every handler by hand. Write it once, apply it everywhere, and every route gets consistent metrics for free.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Watch your label cardinality. Tagging a metric with route and status code is fine, a handful of distinct values. Tagging it with user id or full request path with query strings is not, that can create millions of unique time series and quietly blow up your metrics storage.
5. RED and USE, frameworks for what to instrument
blocks.text: 5. RED and USE, frameworks for what to instrument

blocks.content: Knowing the four metric types doesn't tell you what to actually measure in a real system. RED and USE are two small checklists that answer exactly that question, for two different kinds of things you monitor.
5.1 The RED method
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351172-867663246.png
blocks.alt: RED method: rate, errors, and duration as the three signals for a service

blocks.content: ["Rate, how many requests is this service handling per second","Errors, what fraction of those requests are failing","Duration, how long are requests taking, as a distribution, not an average"]
items: Rate, how many requests is this service handling per second
Errors, what fraction of those requests are failing
Duration, how long are requests taking, as a distribution, not an average

blocks.content: RED is built for request driven services: your API, a payment endpoint, a search service. Anything that takes requests in and sends responses out.
5.2 The USE method
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351173-497862868.png
blocks.alt: USE method: utilization, saturation, and errors as the three signals for a resource

blocks.content: ["Utilization, what percent of the resource's capacity is currently busy","Saturation, how much work is queued up waiting because the resource is already busy","Errors, how many errors this resource itself is throwing"]
items: Utilization, what percent of the resource's capacity is currently busy
Saturation, how much work is queued up waiting because the resource is already busy
Errors, how many errors this resource itself is throwing

blocks.content: USE is built for resources, not services: CPU, disk, memory, network interfaces. Anything with a finite capacity that can run out.

6. Real systems you'll actually run into
blocks.text: 6. Real systems you'll actually run into

blocks.content: The concepts above are universal, but you'll meet them wearing specific names. Three tools come up constantly in interviews and in real production stacks.
6.1 Prometheus
Prometheus is the dominant metrics collection and query system today. Your application exposes a plain HTTP endpoint, usually /metrics, and Prometheus pulls from it on a schedule, called scraping.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351173-569693946.png
blocks.alt: An application exposing a metrics endpoint that Prometheus scrapes on a schedule

blocks.content: Once the data is stored, you query it with PromQL, Prometheus's own query language, built specifically for slicing time series data: rates, sums, percentiles, all of it.
6.2 StatsD

StatsD came earlier and works the opposite way. Your app pushes tiny UDP packets to a StatsD agent every time something happens, instead of waiting to be scraped. It's simpler to set up but needs a separate aggregator to turn all those packets into something queryable.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351174-294402438.png
blocks.alt: Push based StatsD versus pull based Prometheus scraping

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Because StatsD uses UDP, packets can be dropped under load and nobody complains, there's no retry. Prometheus's pull model means a missed scrape is visible as a gap in the data, which is arguably more honest.
6.3 Grafana

Neither Prometheus nor StatsD gives you a nice dashboard out of the box, that's Grafana's job. It connects to your metrics store, runs the queries, and turns the numbers into the graphs, gauges, and alert panels people actually look at.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351174-525290532.png
blocks.alt: Prometheus stores the data, PromQL queries it, Grafana renders the dashboard

blocks.content: 7. Worked example, instrumenting an endpoint
Let's make this concrete. Say you have a Node.js API endpoint and you want to know its request rate, its error rate, and its p99 latency, exactly the RED signals from section 5.
7.1 Adding a counter and a histogram
blocks.text: 7.1 Adding a counter and a histogram

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396351175-479492631.png
blocks.alt: A single request flowing through a counter increment and a histogram observation

blocks.content: Using prom-client, the standard Prometheus client library for Node.js, you define one counter and one histogram, then wrap the route handler so every request updates both.

Notice the counter and histogram are both tagged with route and status code, small fixed sets of values, exactly the kind of low cardinality labels you want. The /metrics route is what Prometheus will scrape.
7.2 Querying p99 latency in PromQL
With the histogram now collecting data, Prometheus's histogram_quantile function turns those raw bucket counts into an actual percentile, computed over any time window you ask for.

histogram_quantile(
  0.99,
  sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/api/orders/:id"}[5m])) by (le)
)

This reads as: take the last 5 minutes of bucket counts, turn them into a per second rate, sum across all instances of this service, then compute the 99th percentile from those buckets. Swap 0.99 for 0.95 or 0.5 and you get p95 or the median instead.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: histogram_quantile needs the _bucket series and the le label, both added automatically by the client library. If you forget rate() over a window first, the query breaks on counter resets from restarts.
8. The interview angle

In a system design interview, nobody expects you to recite PromQL syntax from memory. What they're actually checking is whether you instinctively know what to measure the moment you sketch a new component.

["Say RED out loud for anything that serves requests: rate, errors, duration","Say USE out loud for anything that's a finite resource: utilization, saturation, errors","Call out percentiles, not averages, the moment latency comes up","Name the actual counter or histogram you'd add, don't just say \"we'd add monitoring\""]
items: Say RED out loud for anything that serves requests: rate, errors, duration
Say USE out loud for anything that's a finite resource: utilization, saturation, errors
Call out percentiles, not averages, the moment latency comes up
Name the actual counter or histogram you'd add, don't just say "we'd add monitoring"

blocks.title: What a strong answer sounds like
blocks.text: For a payment service, I'd instrument a request counter split by outcome so I can see success versus decline rate, a duration histogram so I can watch p99 latency on the actual charge call, and on the database side a connection pool gauge so I can catch saturation before it becomes timeouts.

blocks.content: Anyone can say "we'd add monitoring." The candidates who stand out say exactly which counter, which histogram, and which percentile they'd watch, and why.
